person.name: Niels_Bohr
person.summary: Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who explained atomic spectra through quantized electron states and helped establish quantum theory. He built Copenhagen into an international center for theoretical physics, escaped Nazi-occupied Denmark, and later pressed for international cooperation on atomic energy.

conclusion: Later atomic models have supplanted the Bohr model, though its underlying principles remain valid. Bohr’s work also led from Copenhagen to CERN, Risø, and international cooperation on nuclear energy.

events.title: Born into Copenhagen Academic Life
events.description: Niels Bohr is born in Copenhagen as the second of Christian Bohr and Ellen Adler Bohr’s three children. His elder sister Jenny and younger brother Harald grow up with him.

events.title: Begins Physics Studies in Copenhagen
events.description: Bohr enrolled at the University of Copenhagen to study physics. He also studied mathematics, astronomy, and philosophy.

events.title: Defends Thesis on Electron Theory
events.description: Bohr defends his doctoral thesis on the electron theory of metals at the University of Copenhagen. The thesis tests the limits of treating electrons in metals as a gas.
events.background:
At the University of Copenhagen, physics had a small institutional base. When Bohr began his studies, Christian Christiansen was the university's only professor of physics. The university had no physics laboratory for his earlier work on liquid surface tension. He used his father's university laboratory and made the specially shaped glass tubes needed for the experiments himself. His doctoral work grew out of a master's project completed nine months after his brother Harald earned a mathematics master's degree.

The research addressed a major attempt to explain how metals conduct electricity. Paul Drude had proposed that a metal's electrons behave like a gas. Hendrik Lorentz had developed that approach further. Bohr surveyed the available literature and extended Lorentz's model. The calculations still could not account for effects including the Hall effect, in which a magnetic field creates a voltage across a current-carrying conductor. He concluded that electron theory could not fully explain metals' magnetic properties.

The thesis was accepted in April 1911. It drew little interest beyond Scandinavia because the University of Copenhagen required doctoral theses to be written in Danish. Its later history was unusual. In 1921, Dutch physicist Hendrika Johanna van Leeuwen independently derived a result from the thesis. The result is now called the Bohr–van Leeuwen theorem. It states that classical statistical mechanics cannot account for magnetism in materials. The problem Bohr had encountered in trying to explain magnetic behavior had already pointed to that limitation.

events.title: Marries Margrethe Nørlund
events.description: Bohr and Margrethe Nørlund marry in a civil ceremony at Slagelse town hall. They begin their life together in Denmark.

events.title: Joins Rutherford at Manchester Laboratory
events.description: Bohr begins postdoctoral research in Ernest Rutherford’s laboratory at the University of Manchester. He studies Rutherford’s nuclear model of the atom with George de Hevesy and Charles Galton Darwin.

events.title: Publishes Papers on Atomic Structure
events.description: Bohr publishes three papers in Philosophical Magazine. The papers combine Rutherford’s nuclear atom with Planck’s quantum hypothesis and explain hydrogen’s spectral lines.

event_class.title: On the Constitution of Atoms and Molecules
event_class.impact: The model’s underlying principles remain valid despite later atomic models.

events.background:
Atomic theory had a serious stability problem. Rutherford’s 1911 nuclear picture concentrated an atom’s positive charge in a tiny center, yet ordinary physics implied that orbiting electrons should radiate energy and fall inward. The visible lines in hydrogen’s spectrum posed a separate puzzle. Johann Balmer had expressed their wavelengths in a formula in 1885. Later observations supported the formula for three decades without supplying its physical cause.

A further difficulty was the Pickering series, spectral lines that did not fit Balmer’s formula. Alfred Fowler challenged the new account on this point. Bohr replied that the lines came from ionized helium, whose atoms retain only one electron. The same rules used for hydrogen worked for such one-electron helium ions. His treatment also connected the Rydberg constant to measurable quantities including electron mass, electron charge, Planck’s constant, and an atom’s nuclear charge.

Older physicists including J. J. Thomson, Lord Rayleigh, and Hendrik Lorentz disliked the work. Rutherford, David Hilbert, Albert Einstein, Enrico Fermi, Max Born, and Arnold Sommerfeld received it as a breakthrough. Einstein called it “the highest form of musicality in the sphere of thought.” The account earned acceptance because it addressed results that competing atomic pictures had left unexplained and made predictions later tested experimentally. Bohr later identified the number of electrons in an atom’s outer orbits as a major determinant of its chemical properties.

The papers also began a move away from the literal image of tiny planets circling a nucleus. By 1919, Bohr was developing practical rules for atomic behavior. In 1924, Wolfgang Pauli’s exclusion principle gave the electron arrangements a firmer theoretical basis. Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy used those ideas in Copenhagen to find element 72, hafnium, after Bohr had predicted that it would have zirconium-like chemical properties.

events.title: Takes Copenhagen Physics Chair
events.description: Bohr returned to Denmark in 1916 and took the newly created Chair of Theoretical Physics at the University of Copenhagen. He continued teaching physics and researching atomic theory.

events.title: Founds Theoretical Physics Institute
events.description: Bohr opened the Institute of Theoretical Physics at the University of Copenhagen on 3 March 1921 and became its director. The institute hosted researchers including Hans Kramers, Oskar Klein, George de Hevesy, Wojciech Rubinowicz, and Svein Rosseland.

events.title: Receives Nobel Prize in Physics
events.description: Bohr receives the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics in Stockholm. The award recognizes his investigations of atomic structure and the radiation they produce.

events.title: Formulates Complementarity
events.description: Bohr presented the principle of complementarity at the Volta Conference in Como, arguing that quantum objects require wave and particle descriptions in different experimental settings.
events.background:
Quantum theory had acquired two powerful mathematical forms by the mid-1920s. Werner Heisenberg, Max Born, and Pascual Jordan had built matrix mechanics from quantities associated with observable atomic transitions. Erwin Schrödinger had supplied wave mechanics in 1926. Schrödinger’s equations seemed to provide a familiar picture of matter as waves. Paul Dirac spent six months in Copenhagen that year. Heisenberg returned there as a university lecturer and Bohr’s assistant after Hans Kramers left for Utrecht. The group had to decide what the new mathematics said about electrons and light.

Heisenberg had introduced his uncertainty principle in February 1927 through a thought experiment involving a gamma-ray microscope. The imagined microscope used very short-wavelength gamma rays to locate an electron. A photon striking the electron would alter its motion. Heisenberg treated that disturbance as the source of the limits on simultaneous knowledge of position and momentum. Bohr found the argument incomplete. He held that an electron’s position and momentum could not be assigned apart from the arrangement used to measure them. At the Como meeting, he also connected the uncertainty relations to the resolving power of optical instruments. He believed their full meaning required further investigation.

Bohr’s account required physicists to describe the measuring apparatus and its recorded results in the unambiguous terms of classical physics. He later wrote that an experiment must be reportable to others in ordinary language supplemented by classical physical terminology. Albert Einstein preferred the determinism of classical physics and continued to debate these questions with Bohr throughout their lives. The discussions made the foundations of quantum physics a public subject of scientific and philosophical argument.

events.title: Develops the Nuclear Drop Model
events.description: Bohr develops a theory of the compound nucleus in 1936. The theory treats the atomic nucleus as a deformable liquid drop. Fritz Kalckar works with him on the theory.

events.title: Escapes Occupied Denmark
events.description: Word reaches Bohr that German authorities are about to arrest him. He flees from occupied Denmark to Sweden with Margrethe and Aage.
events.background:
Denmark had been under German occupation since April 1940. Bohr’s Institute of Theoretical Physics had already served as a refuge and meeting place for scientists displaced by Nazi rule during the 1930s. The household at the Carlsberg Honorary Residence also lived with a personal danger that Nazi racial policy made immediate. Bohr’s mother, Ellen Adler Bohr, came from a Danish Jewish banking family. The Nazis classified the family as Jewish on that basis.

The danger had acquired another layer after Werner Heisenberg came to Copenhagen in 1941. Heisenberg was then head of the German nuclear weapon project. Margrethe later understood his visit as an attempt to persuade her husband to work with Germany. Bohr did not accept Heisenberg’s intentions. Their meeting damaged a scientific friendship that had grown from Heisenberg’s years at the Copenhagen institute.

The family’s route into exile soon connected them with Allied atomic work. Aage reached Britain in a de Havilland Mosquito operated by British Overseas Airways Corporation. The unarmed aircraft had been converted from a high-speed bomber to carry passengers and valuable cargo. Aage spent its three-hour flight lying on a mattress in the bomb bay, wearing a parachute, flying suit, and oxygen mask. He and his father worked on Britain’s Tube Alloys project under false names. Aage was James Baker and his father was Nicholas Baker.

On 30 December 1943, the two made the first of several visits to the United States. Bohr served there as a consultant to the Manhattan Project. In 1945, J. Robert Oppenheimer asked the Bohrs to review the design of a modulated neutron initiator at Los Alamos. Their conclusion that it would work answered Enrico Fermi’s concerns about the design. The initiators were used in the bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.

events.title: Joins Allied Atomic Work
events.description: Bohr flies from Sweden to Britain under the name Nicholas Baker. He joins the British Tube Alloys project.

events.title: Calls for Atomic Openness
events.description: Bohr publishes an open letter to the United Nations on atomic energy. He urges nations to exchange information and place atomic energy under international control.

events.title: Helps Build Nuclear Research Institutions
events.description: Bohr supports the creation of CERN for European nuclear research. He also helps establish Denmark’s Research Establishment Risø.

events.background:
The postwar research landscape joined questions about atomic nuclei to the practical problem of organizing large laboratories. Bohr had spent the war years connected with the British Tube Alloys project and the British mission to the Manhattan Project. After returning to Denmark, he pressed for international cooperation over atomic energy. His 1950 open letter to the United Nations called for countries to exchange information and place atomic energy under international control. European scientists were also working in a field that required specialized equipment and sustained collaboration across national borders.

Research on the nucleus had already reshaped the work pursued from Copenhagen. In 1936, Bohr and Fritz Kalckar developed the compound-nucleus theory, which treated a nucleus hit by a neutron as a deformable liquid drop. The discovery of nuclear fission brought this line of work new urgency. At a Washington conference in January 1939, Bohr concluded that uranium-235, a rare isotope, was chiefly responsible for fission caused by slow neutrons. John R. Dunning confirmed the prediction experimentally in April 1940. Nuclear research after the war consequently encompassed basic questions about how nuclei behave and the new technologies made possible by fission.

The institutional work placed Danish and European research within this wider scientific community. Copenhagen already had a model in the Institute of Theoretical Physics, which had opened in 1921 and drew researchers including Hans Kramers, Oskar Klein, George de Hevesy, Werner Heisenberg, and Paul Dirac. Bohr later became the first chairman of the Nordic Institute for Theoretical Physics in 1957. CERN provided a common European setting for nuclear research. The Research Establishment Risø served the Danish Atomic Energy Commission. These organizations extended the network of research institutions around Copenhagen beyond the institute that had been associated with Bohr since the 1920s.

events.title: Dies at Home in Copenhagen
events.description: Bohr died at his home in Copenhagen.
